html:
The Roman Senate was the council of Rome's leading men. It advised the kings, steered the Roman Republic for nearly five centuries, and lived on with less power under the emperors. Tradition says Romulus founded it, and it met in the Curia on the Forum.

Senators were mostly former magistrates who sat for life, about 300 of them in the middle Republic. The Senate could not pass laws; the popular assemblies did that. But it controlled money, war, foreign policy and the provinces, and its advice was almost always followed. It also guarded morals: it banned the Bacchanalia in 186 BCE and for a long time blocked permanent theatres in Rome.

The late Republic tested it. Tiberius Gracchus passed his land law over its head and was killed by senators in 133 BCE; against his brother Gaius Gracchus it passed its first "final decree" in 121 BCE. With its backing Cicero crushed Catiline's conspiracy in 63 BCE. Sulla raised it to about 600 members and Caesar to about 900. Julius Caesar was stabbed at a Senate meeting in the hall of the Theatre of Pompey in 44 BCE.

When Octavian became Augustus in 27 BCE, the Senate voted him his powers, and the old forms went on. Under the emperors it became a club of rich nobles and a court for high cases. It faded after the western empire fell; the last record of it in Rome is from the early 600s.
